display_name: Lafage Tessellae Old Vines, Côtes du Roussillon
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Old-vine Grenache and Carignan grown on decomposed schist in Roussillon don’t usually end up on mainstream retail shelves at this price. Lafage pulls these hillside vineyards together, strips out the green notes, and bottles a red that drinks like a Côtes du Rhône but costs significantly less.",
  "wine_summary": "The Tessellae project exists to give broad distribution to Lafage’s estate-grown fruit without the heavy oak treatment or extraction that obscures Roussillon’s native character. The blend runs roughly 40% Grenache, 40% Carignan, and 20% Syrah, sourced from vines averaging sixty years old. Because the estate sits in the Agly valley near Perpignan, the wines inherit a sun-baked ripeness that the winemaking team manages by harvesting earlier than local tradition dictates. The result is a fruit-forward red that keeps its acid line intact and skips the heavy toast notes common in the category. This matters because it proves Roussillon can deliver approachable, everyday drinking wine without sacrificing varietal typicity or site expression.",
  "terroir_expression": "Schist and gneiss dominate the hillside vineyards west of Perpignan, forcing roots deep into fractured bedrock to chase moisture during the dry Mediterranean summers. The Tramontane wind sweeps down from the Pyrenees, stripping humidity from the canopy and naturally thickening grape skins. Those thickened skins translate directly to the glass: you get concentrated dark fruit and a grippy tannic frame without the need for extended maceration. Limestone pockets near the river terraces contribute a chalky minerality that keeps the wine from slipping into jam. Heat accumulation in the Roussillon basin would easily push alcohol past 15%, but the elevation and diurnal temperature shift preserve the fresh black cherry and garrigue herb notes that define the blend.",
  "vinification_summary": "Fermentation happens in temperature-controlled stainless steel and concrete vats, which preserves primary fruit and avoids the vanilla extraction that oak barrels introduce. Lafage uses a short pre-fermentation cold soak—holding crushed grapes at 8–10°C for two days before yeast activity begins—to pull color and stable anthocyanins without leaching harsh seed tannins. Maceration runs just long enough to extract the flesh of the berry while leaving the bitter stems behind, and malolactic fermentation proceeds naturally in tank. The wine is bottled young, usually within eight months, so the tannins stay rounded and the fruit remains forward.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Duck confit with cherry gastrique: the wine’s dark fruit and medium tannins cut through rendered duck fat, while the garrigue herbs mirror the savory thyme in the skin.",
    "Smackover-style pulled pork sandwich: the bright acidity and low-oak profile stand up to tangy vinegar-based barbecue sauce without clashing with smoke.",
    "Lamb shoulder roasted with cumin, smoked paprika, and preserved lemon: the Syrah component handles the spice, and the schist-driven minerality grounds the rich meat.",
    "Wild mushroom and black garlic risotto: earthy umami from the mushrooms meets the wine’s dried herb notes, while the Carignan’s natural acidity lifts the heavy starch."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Domaine Cazes Cuvée Léonie — similar old-vine Grenache/Carignan focus from Roussillon with restrained oak and comparable schist-driven structure.",
    "Château de Beaucastel Coudoulet de Beaucastel — shares the GSM/Carignan framework and Rhône-adjacent profile, though priced higher and showing more Mourvèdre tannic grip.",
    "Mas de Daumas Gassac Red — another Languedoc-Roussillon estate red that punches above its price tier, though it leans heavier into Cabernet and spends longer in barrel."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Medium-to-full-bodied dry red with moderate tannins and sun-warmed dark fruit balanced by schist-driven minerality",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink within three to five years of the vintage to preserve the primary fruit and avoid tannic drying as the wine ages. Store in a cool, dark space at 12–14°C with stable humidity.",
  "value_assessment": "The wine typically retails between $22 and $25 CAD at the LCBO, which puts it directly against Château de la Négly’s La Clape cuvées and basic Côtes du Rhône bottlings from Guigal. It wins on structure and site transparency, delivering more concentration and cleaner acid lines than most entry-level Rhône blends at the same tier. The price reflects bulk production efficiency rather than corner-cutting on vineyard sourcing.",
  "market_position": "Wine directors at mid-tier bistros and independent grocery buyers stock this bottle because it bridges the gap between easy-drinking supermarket reds and terroir-driven natural wines. It appeals to home cooks who want a reliable weeknight pairing that doesn’t require decanting or special glassware. Retailers use it as a volume mover that still earns margin, while sommeliers pull it off the list when customers ask for Rhône-style reds without the Rhône markup.",

parsed.hook: Old-vine Grenache and Carignan grown on decomposed schist in Roussillon don’t usually end up on mainstream retail shelves at this price. Lafage pulls these hillside vineyards together, strips out the green notes, and bottles a red that drinks like a Côtes du Rhône but costs significantly less.
parsed.wine_summary: The Tessellae project exists to give broad distribution to Lafage’s estate-grown fruit without the heavy oak treatment or extraction that obscures Roussillon’s native character. The blend runs roughly 40% Grenache, 40% Carignan, and 20% Syrah, sourced from vines averaging sixty years old. Because the estate sits in the Agly valley near Perpignan, the wines inherit a sun-baked ripeness that the winemaking team manages by harvesting earlier than local tradition dictates. The result is a fruit-forward red that keeps its acid line intact and skips the heavy toast notes common in the category. This matters because it proves Roussillon can deliver approachable, everyday drinking wine without sacrificing varietal typicity or site expression.
parsed.terroir_expression: Schist and gneiss dominate the hillside vineyards west of Perpignan, forcing roots deep into fractured bedrock to chase moisture during the dry Mediterranean summers. The Tramontane wind sweeps down from the Pyrenees, stripping humidity from the canopy and naturally thickening grape skins. Those thickened skins translate directly to the glass: you get concentrated dark fruit and a grippy tannic frame without the need for extended maceration. Limestone pockets near the river terraces contribute a chalky minerality that keeps the wine from slipping into jam. Heat accumulation in the Roussillon basin would easily push alcohol past 15%, but the elevation and diurnal temperature shift preserve the fresh black cherry and garrigue herb notes that define the blend.
parsed.vinification_summary: Fermentation happens in temperature-controlled stainless steel and concrete vats, which preserves primary fruit and avoids the vanilla extraction that oak barrels introduce. Lafage uses a short pre-fermentation cold soak—holding crushed grapes at 8–10°C for two days before yeast activity begins—to pull color and stable anthocyanins without leaching harsh seed tannins. Maceration runs just long enough to extract the flesh of the berry while leaving the bitter stems behind, and malolactic fermentation proceeds naturally in tank. The wine is bottled young, usually within eight months, so the tannins stay rounded and the fruit remains forward.
food_pairing: Duck confit with cherry gastrique: the wine’s dark fruit and medium tannins cut through rendered duck fat, while the garrigue herbs mirror the savory thyme in the skin.
Smackover-style pulled pork sandwich: the bright acidity and low-oak profile stand up to tangy vinegar-based barbecue sauce without clashing with smoke.
Lamb shoulder roasted with cumin, smoked paprika, and preserved lemon: the Syrah component handles the spice, and the schist-driven minerality grounds the rich meat.
Wild mushroom and black garlic risotto: earthy umami from the mushrooms meets the wine’s dried herb notes, while the Carignan’s natural acidity lifts the heavy starch.
comparable_wines: Domaine Cazes Cuvée Léonie — similar old-vine Grenache/Carignan focus from Roussillon with restrained oak and comparable schist-driven structure.
Château de Beaucastel Coudoulet de Beaucastel — shares the GSM/Carignan framework and Rhône-adjacent profile, though priced higher and showing more Mourvèdre tannic grip.
Mas de Daumas Gassac Red — another Languedoc-Roussillon estate red that punches above its price tier, though it leans heavier into Cabernet and spends longer in barrel.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-to-full-bodied dry red with moderate tannins and sun-warmed dark fruit balanced by schist-driven minerality
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink within three to five years of the vintage to preserve the primary fruit and avoid tannic drying as the wine ages. Store in a cool, dark space at 12–14°C with stable humidity.
parsed.value_assessment: The wine typically retails between $22 and $25 CAD at the LCBO, which puts it directly against Château de la Négly’s La Clape cuvées and basic Côtes du Rhône bottlings from Guigal. It wins on structure and site transparency, delivering more concentration and cleaner acid lines than most entry-level Rhône blends at the same tier. The price reflects bulk production efficiency rather than corner-cutting on vineyard sourcing.
parsed.market_position: Wine directors at mid-tier bistros and independent grocery buyers stock this bottle because it bridges the gap between easy-drinking supermarket reds and terroir-driven natural wines. It appeals to home cooks who want a reliable weeknight pairing that doesn’t require decanting or special glassware. Retailers use it as a volume mover that still earns margin, while sommeliers pull it off the list when customers ask for Rhône-style reds without the Rhône markup.
parsed.insider_take: Skip this bottle if you want new-oak vanilla or a heavy, extracted mouthfeel; the winemaking deliberately strips those elements to highlight fruit and soil. It’s the better choice for drinkers who prefer bright acidity and clean finishes over plush, jammy concentration, but it will disappoint anyone looking for a cellar-worthy age-worthy project. Buy it for Tuesday dinners, not for tasting room showpieces.
